name: Morphopsychology

lead: Morphopsychology is a 20th-century method that interprets facial form as a sign of personality. French psychiatrist Louis Corman (1901-1995) coined the term in his 1937 book Quinze leçons de morphopsychologie, arguing that vital forces in the body shape facial forms [1].

For appearance, its relevance is that people use it to read how their facial features may come across to others, and to think about expression and proportions. Related research does show that faces influence first impressions [1].

paras: Practitioners study a face's proportions, bulges and hollows and describe temperament accordingly. It has been applied in psychiatry, employee selection and, in French dentistry, dentofacial orthopedics [7][4][5].
Reading a character from facial structure is classed by academics as pseudoscience, and physiognomy's history includes scientific racism [1]. No physical harm is associated with the practice.

angle.text: Followers use morphopsychology to interpret how face shape and features communicate temperament. Studies of first impressions confirm that observers do attach traits to facial form.

lead: Morphopsychology is a system for relating the shape and details of the face to temperament and psychology. It was developed by the French psychiatrist Louis Corman, who coined the term in 1937 and held that vital forces within the body shape facial forms that in turn reflect psychological traits [1]. A French society still promotes the method [1].

For readers interested in appearance, the framework offers a vocabulary for how facial structure is perceived. Orthognathic-surgery research shows that observers do attribute personality traits to jaw configurations: a scoping review found dysgnathic patients rated more negatively than controls, with ratings improving after surgery [2].

Academics generally classify physiognomy, the broader tradition of judging character from the face, as pseudoscience, though research does find real links between appearance and first impressions, hormones and behavior [1].

paras: Corman's approach reads facial form as the product of vital forces and as a reflection of psychology [1]. A 1977 paper on dentofacial orthopedics described Corman's morphopsychology as the art of relating the shape and features of the face to psychological state, and suggested correlations between deformity type and temperament [3].

Physiognomy has roots in antiquity: Indian and Chinese traditions, then Greek thinkers, and the Physiognomonica attributed to Aristotle's school [1]. Johann Kaspar Lavater's essays from 1772 revived it, and its prestige fell in the late 19th century [1]. A 2024 article on metoposcopy lists morphopsychology among the face-reading vocabularies that grew from this tradition [4]. Mid-20th-century French journals published articles on morphopsychology in psychiatry, industrial psychology and employee selection [5][6][7].

Academics classify physiognomy as pseudoscience because its claims lack solid support [1]. Researchers note genuine connections of another kind: behavior can shape appearance over time, first impressions can create self-fulfilling prophecies, and hormones and gene expression affect both face and personality [1]. A 2020 scoping review of five studies found that observers perceived class II and class III jaw patients differently and that post-surgical ratings improved without reaching control levels in most traits [2].

No studies found testing morphopsychology itself. Related research on how laypeople perceive personality in dysgnathic faces before and after orthognathic surgery is summarized in a 2020 scoping review [2].
